items.title: Null subsets of a smooth manifold
A $C^1$ map is locally Lipschitz on compact coordinate subsets
items.strategy: Cover the compact coordinate subset by finitely many convex balls contained in one chart image, bound the derivative norm on each closed ball by extreme value, and apply the published mean-value inequality on each ball. Chaining across the finite cover avoids using a convexity argument on a nonconvex chart image.

items.title: $C^1$ local diffeomorphisms preserve null sets locally
items.strategy: On compactly contained coordinate pieces, apply the previous lemma to both the map and its inverse to get two Lipschitz bounds. The published Euclidean Lipschitz-image theorem then gives both directions of null-set preservation.

items.title: The manifold null-set definition is independent of the smooth atlas
items.strategy: Reduce an overlap of two atlases to countably many relatively compact coordinate balls and apply local null-set preservation to each transition map. Countable unions close the argument.

items.title: A countable chart cover detects manifold null sets
items.strategy: Use atlas independence to replace the universal quantifier over all charts by any countable smooth atlas with relatively compact domains. The only genuine work is the countable localization, not a new geometric argument.

items.title: Countable unions and subsets of manifold null sets are null
items.strategy: Check nullity in a countable chart cover and appeal chartwise to the Euclidean closure of null sets under subsets and countable unions.

items.title: A null set has dense complement in a positive-dimensional manifold
items.strategy: If a null set contained a nonempty open subset, one chart would contain a nonempty Euclidean open set that was null. That contradicts the Euclidean cube-cover notion of nullity.

items.title: An equidimensional $C^1$ map sends null sets to null sets
items.strategy: Pass to countably many compactly contained coordinate pieces on which the coordinate representative is Lipschitz by the local lemma, and then apply the Euclidean Lipschitz-image theorem.

items.title: The image of a lower-dimensional $C^1$ manifold is null
items.strategy: Refine countable source and target atlases so each source chart maps into one target chart. On each such piece, pad the source chart by a Euclidean factor so that the map becomes equidimensional on the product, then restrict to the zero slice, which is null.

items.title: Positive-codimension immersed submanifolds are null
items.strategy: An immersed submanifold is locally the image of a lower-dimensional manifold under a smooth immersion. Apply the previous proposition chartwise.

items.title: The critical locus and critical value set
Compact null sections imply a compact set is null
items.strategy: Given a compact set in a product, cover each section by finitely many small cubes, thicken the parameter value to a short interval by compactness, and then take a finite subcover in the parameter direction. This is the finite-cover estimate behind Sard's slicing step and avoids an unproved appeal to Fubini for arbitrary sets.

items.title: Sard on the nonflat critical strata
items.strategy: At a point where some derivative first becomes nonzero, use the inverse function theorem to make that derivative a coordinate and then slice by the resulting level hyperplanes. The critical-value set on each slice drops to a smaller-domain Sard problem, and the slicing lemma reassembles the conclusion.

items.title: Sard on the infinitely flat critical stratum
items.strategy: Use Taylor's theorem on tiny cubes around flat points to bound the image of each cube by a target box whose volume decays faster than the domain subdivision count. Summing over the subdivided cubes forces arbitrarily small total target volume.

items.title: Morse-Sard for Euclidean maps
items.strategy: Decompose the critical set into the first nonflat stratum, the higher-order nonflat strata, and the final flat stratum. The first two are handled by the nonflat-strata lemma and induction on the domain dimension; the last by the flat-stratum Taylor estimate. Keep the differentiability threshold explicit as $r>\max\{m-n,0\}$.

items.title: Morse-Sard for smooth manifolds
items.strategy: Localize to a countable smooth atlas of second-countable manifolds and apply the Euclidean theorem in charts. The chart-independence and countable-union nullity results convert the local statement into the intrinsic manifold statement.

items.title: Regular values have null complement and are dense
items.strategy: The complement of the regular-value set is exactly the critical-value set. Apply manifold Sard and then the dense-complement proposition on the target.

items.title: The critical value set of a smooth map is sigma-compact
items.strategy: The critical locus is closed, and a compact exhaustion of the source makes it a countable union of compact sets. Continuous images of those compact pieces are compact in the target.

items.title: Regular values form a dense $G_\delta$ set
items.strategy: Write the critical-value set as a countable union of compact null sets using the previous proposition. Compact null sets have empty interior, so the complement is a countable intersection of dense open sets.

items.title: A smooth map from lower to higher dimension cannot be surjective
items.strategy: If the source dimension is smaller than the target dimension, the whole image is a null subset of the target. A positive-dimensional manifold is not null in any nonempty open set, so surjectivity is impossible.

items.title: Transverse linear subspaces
A smooth map transverse to an embedded submanifold
Transverse smooth maps
Transverse embedded submanifolds
Transversality is equivalent to surjectivity on the normal quotient
items.strategy: Pass from the spanning condition in the tangent space to the quotient by the embedded tangent space. The quotient map kills exactly the submanifold tangent directions, so the image spans the quotient if and only if the original sum is all of the ambient tangent space.

items.title: The transverse preimage theorem
items.strategy: Choose a local defining submersion for the target submanifold and compose it with the map. The quotient-surjectivity criterion turns transversality into submersion of the composite, so the regular-level-set theorem gives the embedded preimage and the tangent-space formula.

items.title: Transverse embedded submanifolds intersect in the expected codimension
items.strategy: Apply the preimage theorem to one inclusion map transverse to the other submanifold. The tangent-space identity follows from the preimage tangent-space description.

items.title: Transverse fibre products are embedded submanifolds
items.strategy: The coincidence set is the preimage of the diagonal under the product map $F\times G$. Because the diagonal is an embedded submanifold and transversality to it is exactly transversality of $F$ and $G$, the preimage theorem applies.

items.title: A submersion is transverse to every embedded submanifold
items.strategy: A surjective differential already spans the ambient tangent space, so the transversality sum condition is automatic.

items.title: Transversality to a point is the regular-value condition
items.strategy: A point has zero tangent space, so the transversality sum condition reduces to surjectivity of the differential at every point of the fibre.

items.title: Transversality is invariant under diffeomorphic changes of source and target
items.strategy: Compose with source and target diffeomorphisms and use the chain rule. The differentials of the diffeomorphisms are linear isomorphisms, so they do not change the spanning condition.

items.title: An $m$-dimensional submanifold transverse to vertical fibres is locally a graph
items.strategy: For an embedded submanifold of the same dimension as the base, transversality to the vertical fibre makes the restricted first projection an isomorphism on tangent spaces. Apply the inverse function theorem to that projection and read the submanifold as a graph in product coordinates.

items.title: A globally one-to-one transverse-fibre submanifold is a graph
items.strategy: The singleton-fibre and transversality hypotheses force the submanifold to have the same dimension as the base. Then the local graph criterion makes the first projection a local diffeomorphism, and bijectivity upgrades it to a global diffeomorphism.

items.title: Smooth families of maps and their evaluation maps
Parametric transversality
items.strategy: Take the preimage $W=\mathcal F^{-1}(Z)$ of the evaluation map and project $W$ to the parameter manifold. Compare surjectivity of that projection on tangent spaces with transversality of the slice, then invoke Sard on the projection.

items.title: Generic translations of a Euclidean-valued map are transverse
items.strategy: Use the family $(p,a)\mapsto f(p)+a$. Its evaluation map is a submersion in the parameter direction, so parametric transversality applies immediately.

items.title: Outside a null set, every translation makes a chosen value a transverse zero
items.strategy: Specialize the previous corollary to the target submanifold consisting of a single point, then rewrite transversality at a point as the regular-value condition.

items.title: Transversality is stable on a compact source
items.strategy: Near points missing the target submanifold, avoidance persists by openness. Near points hitting it, choose a local defining submersion and use openness of the submersion condition for the composed map. Compactness upgrades the local time intervals to one uniform neighborhood.

items.title: Critical points need not be isolated
items.strategy: A constant map has every point critical, so the critical locus can be all of the source.

items.title: The critical-value set need not be closed
items.strategy: A smooth nonproper map can have critical values converging to a regular value. The A-page and B-page examples make the mechanism explicit.

items.title: Sard's theorem does not hold for every $C^1$ map
items.strategy: The differentiability threshold in Morse-Sard is real: Whitney-type $C^1$ examples can have critical values of positive measure.

items.title: Intersecting submanifolds need not be transverse
items.strategy: Coincident tangent lines already violate the spanning condition, even though the set-theoretic intersection is nonempty.

items.title: A preimage need not be a submanifold without transversality
items.strategy: The transverse preimage theorem needs the transversality hypothesis; dropping it allows singular or dimension-jumping fibres.

items.title: Uniform $C^1$ openness of transversality fails on arbitrary noncompact sources
items.strategy: The compact-source stability theorem is the honest statement on this page. Without compact control or the strong topology, perturbations at infinity can destroy transversality.

items.title: Critical points and values of a height function on a sphere
items.strategy: Use the north-south height function on the sphere, compute its differential in ambient coordinates, and identify exactly the two critical points and their critical values.

items.title: A constant map has a large critical locus and one critical value
items.strategy: For a constant map, every differential is zero, so every source point is critical and the image consists of one critical value.

items.title: A smooth map with a nonclosed critical-value set
items.strategy: Build disjoint smooth bumps with critical values approaching a regular value, and verify directly that the limit value has only regular preimages.

items.title: Transverse and tangent intersections of plane curves
items.strategy: Compare a line crossing a parabola with a tangent line at its vertex. The tangent spaces make the transversality difference visible immediately.

items.title: Coordinate spheres intersect as a transverse level set
items.strategy: Write the intersection as the common level set of two smooth functions with independent differentials and apply the transverse-preimage viewpoint.

items.title: A fibre product of submersions
items.strategy: Use two projections to the same Euclidean factor. Their fibre product is an explicit subspace with the predicted dimension.

items.title: Generic affine hyperplanes meet an embedded submanifold transversely
items.strategy: Use translations of a fixed linear functional and apply the generic-translation corollary to the point target in the codomain.

items.title: A map can be vacuously transverse to a submanifold it avoids
items.strategy: Take any smooth map whose image misses the target submanifold. The definition declares transversality automatically.

items.title: A $C^1$ map can have critical values of positive measure
items.strategy: Record the Whitney phenomenon as a sourced Euclidean counterexample to the naive $C^1$ Sard claim, without making its full construction load-bearing on this page.

items.title: A tangent intersection can fail the expected-dimension conclusion
items.strategy: Use tangent plane curves whose intersection multiplicity exceeds the transverse expectation. The set-theoretic fibre is then not the transverse one promised by the theorem.

title: Tensor Fields Exterior Algebra and Differential Forms

items.title: Type $(r,s)$ tensors on a finite-dimensional vector space
The tensor product of multilinear tensors
Tensor product of multilinear tensors is associative and bilinear
items.strategy: Because the page models tensors literally as multilinear maps with ordered argument lists, associativity is equality of formulas rather than a hidden canonical isomorphism. Bilinearity is checked slotwise.

items.title: Permutation action on covariant tensors
Symmetrization and alternation operators
Symmetrization and alternation are projections
items.strategy: Average over the symmetric group and use invariance of the group under left multiplication. The second application of either operator collapses to the first because the averaging has already imposed the symmetry or alternation.

items.title: Contraction of a mixed tensor
Contraction is independent of the basis formula
items.strategy: Write the contraction in a basis and dual basis, then show that a change of basis inserts mutually inverse matrices whose indices collapse to the same intrinsic pairing. This is the exact point where the coordinate formula is justified.

items.title: Pullback of a covariant tensor by a linear map
Linear pullback respects tensor products and permutations
items.strategy: Expand both sides on vectors and compare the resulting multilinear formulas directly. Nothing deeper than the concatenation order and permutation bookkeeping is hidden.

items.title: Alternating $k$-covectors
The wedge product of alternating covectors
The wedge product is alternating and bilinear
items.strategy: Alternation comes from the fibrewise alternation operator and bilinearity from the bilinearity of tensor product and of alternation. The determinant-convention normalization is kept explicit.

items.title: The wedge product is associative and graded-commutative
items.strategy: Use the shuffle formula and the bijection between iterated shuffles and full shuffles for associativity. Graded commutativity is the block-swap sign $(-1)^{k\ell}$.

items.title: The exterior algebra of covectors
Wedge monomials in a dual basis form a basis
items.strategy: Use the determinant formula for basis covectors to show spanning and independence of increasing-index wedges. This is the concrete finite-dimensional basis theorem the later bundle construction needs.

items.title: The dimension of the $k$th exterior power is binomial
items.strategy: Count the increasing $k$-tuples in a basis of an $n$-dimensional space. The same count shows vanishing above dimension.

items.title: The finite-dimensional exterior power of vectors
The finite-dimensional exterior power has the universal property
items.strategy: Define the factorization on the wedge basis and verify that it gives the required alternating map on decomposable wedges. Uniqueness follows because those wedges span the exterior power.

items.title: Finite-dimensional exterior powers are functorial
items.strategy: Compose alternating multilinear maps with a linear map in each slot and then invoke uniqueness in the universal property. Identity and composition are checked on decomposable wedges.

items.title: Exterior powers carry a canonical duality pairing
items.strategy: Evaluate an alternating covector on a decomposable wedge and compute the resulting determinant in a basis. Basis independence comes from the dual-basis wedge theorem.

items.title: The top exterior power is one-dimensional
items.strategy: Apply the basis theorem in top degree. The determinant pairing singles out the unique basis vector up to scale.

items.title: Interior product on alternating covectors
Interior product is a graded antiderivation
items.strategy: Expand the wedge formula on vectors and separate the terms in which the inserted vector lands in the left or right factor. The sign comes from moving the inserted slot past the left block.

items.title: The type $(r,s)$ tensor bundle
Tensor transition laws define a smooth vector bundle
items.strategy: Write the coordinate change on one tangent slot and one cotangent slot, then take the ordered tensor product of those matrices over all slots. The cocycle identity is inherited from the tangent and cotangent transition identities.

items.title: Smooth tensor fields
Smoothness of a tensor field is equivalent to smooth coordinate components
items.strategy: Use the local frame of tensor-coordinate monomials from a coordinate chart and apply the published criterion for smooth sections in a vector bundle.

items.title: Tensor products and contractions of smooth tensor fields are smooth
items.strategy: In local coordinates the tensor product and contraction are polynomial expressions in the component functions. Smoothness of the components then proves smoothness of the resulting field.

items.title: Pullback of a covariant tensor field
Pullback of covariant tensor fields is smooth and functorial
items.strategy: Smoothness is checked in coordinates by substitution of the Jacobian entries, and functoriality is the chain rule lifted from the linear pullback formula.

items.title: A general mixed tensor field does not pull back along every smooth map
items.strategy: Contravariant slots would require pushing tangent vectors forward through an inverse map, and a general smooth map does not provide that data.

items.title: Symmetric and alternating covariant tensor subbundles
Symmetric and alternating images are smooth subbundles
items.strategy: Symmetrization and alternation are fibrewise projections of constant rank. The image and kernel of a constant-rank bundle map are smooth subbundles.

items.title: The exterior power bundle of the cotangent bundle
Exterior power transition laws define a smooth vector bundle
items.strategy: Either take exterior powers of the cotangent transition matrices directly or identify the bundle as the alternating subbundle of covariant tensors. The latter gives the smoothness and rank in one step.

items.title: Smooth differential $k$-forms
A differential form has a unique local coordinate expression
items.strategy: Use the wedge basis in the cotangent fibre and the section smoothness criterion to identify the coefficient functions. Uniqueness is fibrewise linear independence of the basis wedges.

items.title: The wedge product of differential forms
Differential forms form a graded-commutative algebra
items.strategy: All algebraic laws are fibrewise laws already proved for alternating covectors, and smoothness is preserved because the wedge coefficients are polynomial in the coordinate components.

items.title: Interior product of a form by a vector field
Interior product on forms is a graded antiderivation
items.strategy: Apply the fibrewise antiderivation identity pointwise and observe that the result varies smoothly because both the vector field and the form are smooth.

items.title: Pullback of a differential form
Pullback of forms is smooth, functorial, and preserves wedges
items.strategy: This is the covariant tensor pullback restricted to alternating tensors. Functoriality comes from the tensor pullback, and wedge preservation from the linear pullback formula on alternating covectors.

items.title: A diffeomorphism pulls back tensor fields and forms isomorphically
items.strategy: Use the inverse diffeomorphism and functoriality to build the inverse pullback. For mixed tensors, combine the pullback on covariant slots with the pushforward induced by the inverse on contravariant slots.

items.title: The wedge product is not commutative
items.strategy: The correct law is graded commutativity, and one-forms already change sign under swapping.

items.title: A nonzero one-form wedges with itself to zero
items.strategy: Graded commutativity gives $\alpha\wedge\alpha=-\alpha\wedge\alpha$ for a one-form, so the square vanishes.

items.title: Forms of degree above dimension vanish
items.strategy: The alternating fibre in degree greater than the dimension is zero by the basis count.

items.title: Tensor components do not transform as independent scalars
items.strategy: Coordinate changes act by Jacobian and inverse-Jacobian matrices on the respective slots, so the component functions are coupled.

items.title: A general tensor is not determined by diagonal values alone
items.strategy: Diagonal evaluation only detects polarized data under symmetry or alternation hypotheses. A general bilinear map can vanish on all diagonal pairs and still be nonzero.

title: Tensor Fields Exterior Algebra and Differential Forms — Examples

items.title: Tensor product and contraction in a basis
items.strategy: Write explicit basis components for a simple mixed tensor, take its tensor product with a covector, and contract a chosen pair of slots to make the index bookkeeping concrete.

items.title: A bilinear form as a type $(0,2)$ tensor
items.strategy: Interpret a familiar bilinear form directly as a covariant tensor and read off its matrix of components.

items.title: An endomorphism as a type $(1,1)$ tensor
items.strategy: Identify a linear endomorphism with the corresponding mixed tensor and evaluate it on a covector-vector pair.

items.title: The identity endomorphism and its coordinate-independent trace
items.strategy: View the identity as a type $(1,1)$ tensor, contract its slots, and recover the dimension as the trace in any basis.

items.title: Wedge products of the standard dual basis
items.strategy: Compute low-degree wedges of basis covectors and verify the sign change under swapping slots.

items.title: Determinant as the pairing of top exterior powers
items.strategy: Evaluate a top-degree covector on a decomposable top wedge and identify the determinant formula explicitly.

items.title: The Euclidean metric as a symmetric two-tensor
items.strategy: Write the Euclidean inner product as a smooth symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor field and note the symmetry through the fibrewise projection.

items.title: The area form in polar coordinates
items.strategy: Pull back $dx\wedge dy$ along polar coordinates and expand using the pullback and wedge formulas to get $r\,dr\wedge d\theta$.

items.title: Pullback of the circle angular form along a parametrized curve
items.strategy: Evaluate the pullback of a concrete one-form along a curve and read it as an ordinary differential in the parameter.

items.title: A vector field need not admit a pullback under a noninjective map
items.strategy: Use a noninjective smooth map whose two source points would force incompatible target vectors at one image point. This is exactly the obstruction behind the mixed-tensor pullback false statement.

items.title: A reflection changes the sign of a top-degree coordinate form
items.strategy: Pull back a top-degree coordinate form along a reflection and compute the resulting sign flip from the determinant of the Jacobian.

items.title: The canonical one-form on a cotangent bundle
items.strategy: At a cotangent vector, evaluate a tangent vector by projecting to the base and then applying the cotangent vector to that projection. This makes the tautological one-form a concrete covariant tensor field before the exterior derivative is introduced later.
